tips.text: Keeping your bottles where you eat makes them easier to remember.
Missed one? Follow your label or ask a pharmacist. Don't double up.
Some supplements are better absorbed with food. Your label usually says.
A consistent time each day tends to stick better than a perfect time.
Bringing a new supplement into the mix? It's worth a quick check with your pharmacist.
You can pick how many nudges you get in Profile. Choose the reminder style that fits your day.
Check expiration dates now and then, especially for probiotics and oils.
Keep a list of everything you take, supplements included. Review it with your clinician or pharmacist now and then.
A weekly pill organizer can make it easy to see what you've already taken today.
Natural doesn't always mean safe. Some herbal products can interact with medicines.
Having surgery? Tell your care team about every supplement you take, since some can affect bleeding or anesthesia.
Pregnant or breastfeeding? Check with your clinician before taking supplements beyond a standard prenatal.
The FDA doesn't approve supplements before they're sold. Your pharmacist can help you compare products.
Be careful with products sold for weight loss, sexual enhancement, or bodybuilding. Some have been found to contain hidden drug ingredients.
The Supplement Facts label lists each ingredient and the amount per serving. It's the best place to check what's in your product.
The same nutrient can show up in more than one product, like a multivitamin and a single vitamin. Checking your labels helps you know your total.
If you have a bad reaction to a supplement, talk with your clinician. You can also report it to the FDA.
Supplements can't take the place of a varied diet. Foods provide more than vitamins and minerals.
Store supplements out of children's reach, especially gummies that look like candy.
Taking prescription medicines? Your pharmacist can check your supplements for interactions.
Switching brands? Amounts can differ between products, so give the new label a quick read.
Tell each of your clinicians about the supplements you take, not only the one who suggested them.
Vitamin D is fat-soluble, so a meal with some fat helps your body absorb it.
Vitamin C helps your body absorb iron from plant foods like beans and greens.
Keep iron supplements, including multivitamins with iron, out of children's reach. Accidental iron overdose is dangerous for young kids.
Calcium carbonate is absorbed best with food, while calcium citrate works with or without it. Your label says which one you have.
Taking warfarin? Check with your clinician before starting or stopping vitamin K, since it can change how the medicine works.
Biotin can throw off some lab tests. Let your clinician know you take it before any blood work.
Magnesium supplements can cause loose stools for some people. Your label has the directions for your form.
Studies have found that many melatonin products contain a different amount than the label says. A pharmacist can help you pick a product.
St. John's wort interacts with many medicines. If you take any prescription, check with your pharmacist first.
Ginkgo may raise bleeding risk for people on blood thinners. Check with your clinician if you take one.
Garlic supplements may raise bleeding risk. Mention them to your care team before any surgery.
Fiber supplements like psyllium need plenty of liquid. Your label says how much.
Caffeine adds up across coffee, tea, energy drinks, and supplements. Checking labels helps you know your daily total.
Creatine usually causes a little weight gain because your muscles hold more water.
Some probiotics need the fridge and others don't. Your label says how to store yours.
Fish oil side effects are usually mild, like an aftertaste or heartburn. Your label has the directions for your product.
Too much preformed vitamin A during pregnancy can harm a baby. If you're pregnant, review your labels with your clinician.
High amounts of vitamin B6 from supplements over a long time can cause nerve problems. Checking your labels helps you know your total.
Taking a lot of zinc for a long time can lower copper levels. Your labels show how much zinc you get in total.
Beta-alanine can cause a tingling or prickling feeling in the skin. Your label has the directions for your product.
Liver injury has been reported, though rarely, with green tea extract pills. Check with your clinician if you have liver concerns.
Ashwagandha should be avoided during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Your clinician can help if you have questions.
